book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today

chapters.file: ch07 - How to Use this Book in a Philosophy Course.md
ch09 - The Talking Cure for Our Culture.md
chapters.relation: Young argues that South Park, like Socrates in Plato's Apology, is accused of corrupting youth and impiety but is really a philosophical gadfly. Kyle and Stan reach moral conclusions (e.g., refusing to kill Stan's grandfather) through Socratic questioning and dialogue, while Cartman's thoughtless, imitative cruelty mirrors Arendt's banality of evil in Eichmann. Young reads the show's vulgarity through Freud, arguing its crude jokes release repressed drives so we can examine them, making the show a Socratic 'talking cure' for a mindless culture.

Arp uses cartoon Johnnie Cochran's 'Chewbacca Defense' from 'Chef Aid' to teach basic logic: the structure of arguments (premises and conclusion), premise/conclusion indicators, and the difference between deductive validity and inductive strength, illustrated with Cartman's tooth-fairy and Towelie arguments. The Chewbacca Defense is a red-herring fallacy, and other episodes illustrate hasty generalization, slippery slope, false dilemma, appeal to inappropriate authority, and ad hominem. Arp argues South Park deliberately violates logical principles to expose the absurdity and real harm of bad reasoning.

Johnson uses Stephen Colbert's coinages to refute relativism and gut-thinking. 'My Truth' represents individual relativism and 'Wikiality' cultural relativism, both of which Johnson rejects via the correspondence theory of truth and counterexamples like slavery and Nazi Germany. 'Truthiness' is intuitionism, which Johnson attacks using Locke's critique of 'enthusiasts' who reason in a circle, and he argues that appeals to 'a right to my opinion' reveal indifference to truth. Following Socrates, he concludes we should defend beliefs with argument and admit ignorance rather than trust the gut.

chapters.file: ch13 - Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress.md
chapters.relation: Jacoby uses Stan Marsh as the embodiment of W. K. Clifford's ethics of belief, that it is always wrong to believe on insufficient evidence. Stan debunks TV psychic John Edward, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the one making extraordinary claims. Jacoby distinguishes evidential from prudential reasons, presents and criticizes Pascal's Wager (using 'Cartmanland' and the problem of undeserved suffering), and argues via Clifford that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken the mind and, as Stan tells Edward, slow 'the progress of all mankind.'

Lawrence uses The Matrix to raise Cartesian skepticism: Neo's deception dramatizes Descartes's dream argument and evil demon, the computer-run Matrix being a technological version of the demon. He argues even Morpheus cannot be certain he has truly awakened ('the Matrix within the Matrix'), so the only certainty is Descartes's cogito. Drawing on Russell's 'Appearance and Reality,' he then argues that even setting aside Matrix scenarios, naive realism fails, since a chair's color, texture, solidity and shape are all perception-relative, leaving the external world's nature deeply uncertain.

chapters.file: ch15 - “You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”.md
chapters.relation: Silverman uses Battlestar Galactica to explore knowledge as justified true belief. Adama's 'true lie' about knowing Earth's location makes Starbuck's belief in Earth a Gettier case, a justified true belief resting on false justification. He tests Adama's testimony against Goldman's reliabilism (sight is unreliable for spotting Cylons; memory deceives Boomer and Tigh) and Hume's skepticism about testimony versus Plantinga's defense of it. Finally, against Clifford's evidentialism he deploys William James's 'will to believe,' arguing that faith in Earth is a forced, momentous choice that gives the Colonials purpose.

chapters.file: ch17 - The Role of Matter Biology or Function.md
chapters.relation: Lawrence uses The Matrix to survey theories of mind. Neo's apparent mind-body separation fits Descartes's dualism, but Lawrence argues dualism fails on the interaction problem and lack of evidence, so the Matrix scenario supports materialism. He explains reductive (identity) and eliminative materialism (via Churchland and the Tastee Wheat question), then frames the biology-versus-function debate: Searle's emergent-property view (the beer-can thirst model) holds brain biochemistry is essential to consciousness, while functionalism (Lewis's Martian pain) holds any system with the right input-output relations has mental states, and Lawrence argues functionalism underlies the very idea of sentient machines like Agent Smith.

Southworth uses Wolverine and other X-Men to examine personal identity. Locke's memory criterion (illustrated by the Cassandra Nova/Xavier mind-swap and connected memories) implies that Wolverine's repeated amnesia makes him literally several successive persons until House of M restores all his memories. Jamie Madrox's up-to-100 duplicates function as a real-world version of Parfit's fission thought experiment, showing sameness of memory is insufficient for identity. Southworth applies Parfit's brain-based, seven-year view to Wolverine's constant healed head trauma and concludes we should be slow to judge characters as the 'same' culpable person.

chapters.file: ch19 - Time Travel and Fixed Time.md
chapters.relation: Pierce uses Harry Potter's prophecies to analyze destiny, fixed time, and freedom. Distinguishing Trelawney's fraudulent fortune-telling from her two genuine prophecies, he classifies kinds of prophecy (fallible, infallible, self-fulfilling) and, drawing on Aristotle's sea-battle problem and Alexander of Aphrodisias, argues Voldemort's choice of Harry rather than the prophecy itself made it true. He then sorts compatibilist and libertarian readings of Rowling's denial of destiny, argues her time travel (saving Buckbeak) implies a fixed view of time consistent with relativity, and suggests the improbable luck fulfilling prophecies hints at providential guidance.

chapters.file: ch20 - “Cyborgs Don’t Feel Pain. I Do.”.md
chapters.relation: Littmann uses the Terminator films to ask whether machines can be persons. The Terminators clearly pass the Turing Test by convincingly passing for human, giving behavioral evidence that they think. Littmann then presses Searle's Chinese Room, reworked as a tiny non-English-speaking Austrian inside the T-101 reciting phonetic lines, to argue that behavior alone cannot prove genuine understanding or feeling. He concludes that the films' 'Terminator's-eye-view' shots, showing the world from the machine's perspective, are the strongest evidence that the machines are conscious and so may count as people surviving humanity's extinction.

chapters.file: ch22 - Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy.md
chapters.relation: Johnson uses 'Cartmanland' to lay out the problem of evil: Kyle loses his faith when the wicked Cartman gains perfect happiness, giving a logical problem-of-moral-evil argument against God. Johnson shows why the story of Job and Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' fail, then explains the greater-good and free-will defenses (invoking Augustine that only free acts are good) and the residual problem of natural evils like Kyle's hemorrhoid. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by South Park's Jesus, that God permits both moral and natural evil so we develop character, while noting the surviving evidential problem of evil's sheer amount.

Gallagher uses Lost's Rose Henderson, who says 'I just know,' to expound Aquinas on faith and reason. Aquinas places faith midway between Plato's knowledge (epistêmê) and opinion (doxa) and distinguishes its material object (God) from its formal object (first truth). Gallagher explains that all knowledge begins in the senses, so God's existence is known only by demonstration (the five ways), while faith's fuller content requires grace. Rose's sins bracket the argument: Charlie's despair is acedia, while Rose's insistence that she 'knows' the island cured her is presumption, mistaking faith for scientific knowledge.

chapters.file: ch24 - “You Have to Believe in Something”.md
chapters.relation: Eberl and Vines use Battlestar Galactica's Baltar, Six, Adama and Roslin to debate God's existence and meaning. Against Baltar's scientific naturalism they present Aquinas's five ways (unmoved mover, first cause, and the argument from design applied to the universe's ordered laws) and dismiss Pascal's Wager as insincere, like Baltar's. They then raise the problem of evil, answering with Augustine's free-will defense and Hick's soul-making theodicy against Hume's faulty-architect analogy. Finally, contrasting Russell's meaning-amid-a-godless-cosmos with religious faith, they argue atheism need not entail nihilism and that survival and human solidarity give the Colonials common ground.

chapters.file: ch26 - But Isn’t It Only Natural.md
chapters.relation: Adams uses the superpowered characters of Heroes to teach Plato's Republic. The Ring of Gyges question, whether one with the power to escape consequences has reason to be just, is posed by Sylar, Daphne, and Hiro cheating in Vegas. Adams maps Plato's tripartite soul, thumos, logistikon, and epithumetikon, onto Claire's courage and wisdom and Sylar's ruinous intemperance, arguing justice is psychic health so vices grow worse the more power one has. He adds the 'Pagan Golden Rule' (help friends, harm enemies) to read Claire's apology to Brody, concluding virtue is natural to a well-ordered human soul and is its own reward.

McAleer uses the British Office to teach Aristotle's virtue ethics, treating wit as a character virtue that is a mean between the vices of buffoonery (excess) and boorishness (deficiency). David Brent is the buffoon, slave to his need to be thought funny; Gareth Keenan the literalist boor who cannot take or get a joke; and Tim Canterbury the ready-wit whose ironic humor is appropriate to circumstance. McAleer argues wit shows Aristotle's morality is broader than duty or outcome, aiming at eudaimonia, and that humor's uncodifiability, like Wittgenstein's remarks, mirrors how virtue requires practical wisdom rather than rules.

White asks why Batman won't kill the Joker, framing it through utilitarianism (killing one to save the Joker's many future victims) versus deontology (killing is wrong regardless of consequences). Using Foot and Thomson's trolley and transplant cases, plus agent-neutral versus agent-relative rules, he notes key disanalogies: the Joker is not a moral innocent but the very cause of the danger, which pushes toward killing him. But because future killings are only probable, doing so would be 'prepunishment,' and White, a self-described deontologist, concludes it is genuinely hard to say Batman is right, though he admires the restraint.

Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as a would-be consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) whose plan to kill millions to end the Cold War exposes utilitarianism's neglect of rights and, via Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ends,' its dependence on an unknowable infinite future. Rorschach poses as a Kantian deontologist ('I shall not compromise') but Loftis shows his hypocrisy, black-and-white dichotomous thinking, and failure to respect persons betray Kant's categorical imperative. Loftis argues neither theory is truly held by either character; both are rationalizations of power, and the comic's real target, captured by 'Who watches the watchmen?', is authoritarianism itself.
